title: Tea and death
hook: death cafés, begun in London, invite plain talk about death over tea
carry: permission to say it out loud

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was near-death experiences, read two ways by careful people. Your line was not settled. Today, strangers sit down and talk about death on purpose.

A sign on a café door: death café tonight, all welcome. Inside, a handful of strangers around a few tables pushed together. A pot of tea. A plate of cake. A retired teacher, a nursing student, a man whose father died in the spring, a woman whose last birthday rattled her more than she expected. Nobody is selling anything. Nobody is leading a lesson. Someone pours, and someone else asks: has anyone here ever sat with a person while they died? And slowly, the room starts talking.
screen: `A SIGN ON THE DOOR.` → `STRANGERS, TEA, CAKE.` → `DEATH AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: A man in London named Jon Underwood began hosting what he called death cafés, and he credited the idea to the Swiss sociologist Bernard Crettaz, who had held gatherings he called cafés mortels. Underwood published a simple guide so anyone could host one, and the idea traveled. The rules are few. A death café has no agenda and no set topic. It isn't a grief support group, and it isn't counseling. Nobody is trying to lead anyone to a conclusion, a product or a belief. The stated aim, as the organizers put it, is to help people make the most of their lives by talking about death. And there's something to eat and drink. Why does the tea matter? Food and drink make it ordinary. It's hard to whisper about the unspeakable while someone is asking if you want milk. A cup gives your hands something to do in the pauses, and the cake says this is a gathering of people, not a seminar. People come with all sorts of views: religious, not religious, unsure. A Catholic and an atheist can sit at the same table and both be heard. Some come because someone has died. Some come because nobody in their life will talk about it. Some come out of curiosity and stay late. Across these weeks, traditions have spoken about death. A death café adds something simple: permission to say it out loud, in daylight, between sips.
screen: `A LONDON IDEA, FROM SWITZERLAND.` · `NO AGENDA, NO SELLING.` · `WHY THE TEA MATTERS.` · `EVERY VIEW AT ONE TABLE.` · then, large: `TEA AND DEATH.`

segments.voice: Choose one person you could talk to about death, someone easy, not someone hard, and one gentle question a death café might start with: what would you want your last day to look like, who do you miss most, does death scare you? Let the question settle until it feels like something you could actually say, maybe over tea.
Death café, gatherings where strangers talk plainly about death over tea and cake, with no agenda and nothing to sell. Today's word.
Your line: permission to say it out loud. A cup of tea makes room for the hardest talk. That's day seven hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Death cafés are hosted by volunteers in cafés, homes and community spaces; people gather over tea and cake to talk about death with no agenda, and the gatherings are not grief support or counseling.
